title: Authorization
description: Compare RBAC, ABAC, and ReBAC authorization models, learn policy-as-code with OPA/Rego, and understand Google Zanzibar — the system behind Google Drive, YouTube, and Cloud IAM permissions.

segments.text: Authentication answers who are you. Authorization answers what can you do. At scale, authorization is harder. A simple role check becomes a nightmare when you have hierarchical organizations, shared resources, and cross-tenant permissions. Google checks authorization two trillion times per day across their services.

RBAC — Role-Based Access Control — is the most common model. Users have roles, roles have permissions. Admin can read/write/delete, viewer can only read. Simple and easy to audit. But it gets rigid fast. What if you need 'editor who can only edit documents in their department created in the last thirty days'? RBAC can't express that without role explosion.

ABAC — Attribute-Based Access Control — solves role explosion. Policies reference attributes of the user, resource, action, and environment. 'Allow if user.department equals resource.department AND action is edit AND time is within business_hours.' Flexible but complex — policies become hard to reason about and audit as they grow.

Open Policy Agent with Rego enables policy-as-code. Write authorization rules in Rego, deploy them alongside your services, and evaluate them at runtime. Policies are version-controlled, testable, and auditable. Netflix uses OPA to enforce access policies across their entire microservice fleet — one policy engine, hundreds of services.

Consider Google Drive. User A shares a folder with User B. User B can see all files in the folder, including files added later. This isn't RBAC or ABAC. What model captures these relationship-based permissions?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you model Google Drive sharing permissions? Roles alone aren't enough.

segments.text: Google Zanzibar is a Relationship-Based Access Control system — ReBAC. It stores object-to-user relationships as tuples: document:readme, viewer, user:alice. Permissions propagate through relationships — if alice is a member of engineering group, and engineering has viewer access to a folder, alice can view all documents in that folder.

Zanzibar handles ten million authorization checks per second with sub-millisecond latency. It achieves this through aggressive caching of relationship lookups and a concept called zookies — opaque tokens that guarantee read-after-write consistency. SpiceDB and Authzed are open-source implementations inspired by the Zanzibar paper.

Airbnb built Himeji — their authorization service — after outgrowing RBAC. A host can manage their listing, a co-host has limited management rights, a guest has booking rights, and Airbnb support has emergency override. These relationships don't fit roles — they're contextual to each resource. Himeji processes over one hundred thousand checks per second.

The tradeoff matrix: RBAC is simple, auditable, but rigid — use for internal tools. ABAC is flexible but complex to debug — use when attributes drive access. ReBAC handles shared resources and hierarchies — use for multi-tenant, collaborative apps. Most real systems combine all three at different layers.

You're designing authorization for a document collaboration platform like Google Docs. Users can share with individuals, groups, or via link. Permissions include view, comment, and edit. Which authorization model would you choose and why?
segments.thought_prompt: Design authorization for a Google Docs-like platform. Which model handles sharing with individuals, groups, and links?

segments.text: Authorization is the unsung hero of system security. RBAC for simple access control, ABAC with OPA for policy-driven decisions, and ReBAC via Zanzibar for relationship-based permissions. The Staff-level pattern: centralize authorization into a dedicated service early. Embedding auth logic across services creates inconsistent enforcement and audit nightmares.
